Squares, Circles, and Triangles

InvariantsLogic
Game: pick two different shapes. With elimination they become one of the third kind; without, both become the third kind. Aim for one shape (or all the same).
How to play: tap two different shapes. Use Reset for a new row, Repeat for the same start.
Look for the math

Only the counts of each shape matter. Write them as a triple (s, c, t). Every move changes that triple in a tight way, and an invariant decides which endings are possible.

With elimination

A move turns two different shapes into one of the third kind, so the counts change by (−1,−1,+1) in some order. Differences of any two counts stay the same modulo 2, and each count flips parity every move. A lone triangle therefore needs s ≡ c (mod 2) — the page’s necessary condition — but that is not always enough (two squares already match a parity filter for a lone circle, yet no move exists). The logic test checks the mod-2 invariant on every small board and that every reachable finish satisfies the full parity filter.

Without elimination

Both chosen shapes become the third kind: counts change by (−1,−1,+2). Differences are invariant modulo 3. A row of only triangles needs s ≡ c (mod 3). The same idea is the three-colour chameleon puzzle (Kvant / Tournament of Towns).

Getting there

When the invariant allows an ending, a short search usually finds a path — try a small Random deal with Elimination on, and watch which counts keep the same parity.

Start with 4 shapes and Elimination. Can you finish on a triangle?
